authority: Head, Bloch, Hastings, Bourque, Cadena, Herrera, Polly & Jaramillo, 2009

overview.text: Titanoboa is an extinct relative of today's boas from the Paleocene of Colombia, known only from fossil vertebrae and ribs. Estimated at about 13 m long and over a tonne, it is the largest snake known.

fossils.text: Vertebrae and ribs from the Cerrejón coal mine in north-eastern Colombia, belonging to 28 individuals. It was named in 2009.

geology.text: The fossils come from the Cerrejón Formation, dated to about 58 to 60 million years ago (middle to late Paleocene) - some 6 to 8 million years after the non-bird dinosaurs died out.

size.text: From the size of its vertebrae, compared with living boas, its describers estimated a body length of about 13 m and a mass of about 1,135 kg. These are estimates, not measurements of a complete skeleton.

uncertainty.text: Its describers argued that a snake this large needed a mean annual temperature of at least 30 to 34 °C, so the Paleocene tropics were hotter than today. Other scientists questioned whether today's snakes' temperature limits can be scaled up to Titanoboa, and whether a small sample of backbones shows the species' usual size.

nature.title: Giant boid snake from the Palaeocene neotropics reveals hotter past equatorial temperatures
nature.authors: Head, Bloch, Hastings, Bourque, Cadena, Herrera, Polly & Jaramillo

npr.title: 1-ton snakes once slithered in the tropics
